To handle dense grids and memory constraints [S1]:

The claim states that the evidence supports the idea that the method handles dense grids and memory constraints. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that the hierarchical application of the pruning algorithm 'reduces memory footprint' and allows the method to 'scale gracefully to large scenes... that would not be possible otherwise due to memory constraints.' It also notes that applying pruning directly to all cells of a dense grid without hierarchy may cause memory allocation to fail, implying the hierarchical approach is the solution to this problem. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim.

Unlike bounding-volume approaches that require boxes extended by the blending radius, Lipschitz Pruning is space-centric, requires no bounding box computation, and guarantees distance exactness [S1].

The evidence supports all parts of the claim. 1. 'Space-centric': The text describes the algorithm as reducing active nodes 'for a specific region of space (e.g., a grid cell)' and using a 'hierarchical' approach on a grid. 2. 'Requires no bounding box computation': The text explicitly contrasts the method with 'range arithmetic (affine/interval)' which is described as 'more costly', stating that 'Lipschitz bounds use a single evaluation to estimate bounds on a region' instead. While it mentions a 'bounding sphere' for the region in the skip condition, it does not require computing bounding boxes for the primitives themselves in the way traditional bounding-volume approaches do; it relies on the Lipschitz property. 3. 'Guarantees distance exactness': The text states the method is for 'exact and conservative SDFs' and that the pruning produces a 'pruned tree equivalent to the full tree within that region', preserving 'exact distance values'. The far-field culling is noted as 'not exact' but a lower bound, but the core pruning algorithm guarantees exactness.
supported
High blending radius $k$ negatively affects runtime [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes section: 'k: Blending radius used in smooth CSG operators. Impacts the range at which a primitive can be pruned; higher values negatively affect runtime.' Additionally, the mathematical condition for skipping an operator is $|f_1(p) - f_2(p)| ≥ k + 2R$. A higher $k$ increases the threshold required to skip an operator, meaning fewer operators will be skipped/pruned, leading to more computations and thus negatively affecting runtime.

Determine the global state and construct the pruned tree [S1].

Furthermore, the evidence states that this process effectively builds a 'pruned tree' valid for the region by rewiring parents and dropping unused sub-trees.

It relies on the 1-Lipschitz property of the distance function to determine if a binary operator's result is unaffected by blending within a spatial region [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the pruning algorithm 'relies on the 1-Lipschitz property' to determine if a binary operator can be skipped (pruned). Specifically, the text notes: 'We take advantage of the fact that all the expressions are 1-Lipschitz: we detect binary operators that can be safely skipped... if |f1(p)−f2(p)| ≥ k+2R it follows that |f1−f2| ≥ k for all points in this region... This implies that we can replace the operator with one of its children'. This confirms that the 1-Lipschitz property is used to determine if the operator's result is unaffected by blending (i.e., reduces to a single operand) within the spatial region.
